1:1: Silvanus is the Latin form of “Silas.” Silvanus is the name of a man, the same person listed in the book of Acts as Paul’s fellow traveler.
Although Paul wrote this letter, he identifies Silvanus and Timothy as also sending it. This means that they were with him and were in agreement with it.
ἐν Θεῷ Πατρὶ ἡμῶν καὶ Κυρίῳ Ἰησοῦ Χριστῷ
Here Paul speaks of the believers as though they were occupying space inside of God and Jesus. This metaphor expresses the idea that believers are spiritually united to God and Jesus.
1:2: Many languages have different ways to offer good wishes as they greet. Paul greeted his letter recipients with a blessing.
1:3: General Information: In verses 3–12, Paul gives thanks for the believers in Thessalonica and prays for them. A heading for this section might be, “Thanks and Prayers.”
Paul here uses the word ought to express that he has a moral obligation to God to give thanks for the believers in Thessalonica.
Paul uses always as a generalization meaning “often” or “regularly.”
1:4: Here, ourselves is added to we to emphasize that even the apostle Paul and his associates are boasting about the Thessalonian believers.
ἐν πᾶσιν τοῖς διωγμοῖς ὑμῶν, καὶ ταῖς θλίψεσιν
The two words persecutions and afflictions are saying very similar things. The repetition is used to emphasize how difficult life has been for the Thessalonian believers.
πίστεως ἐν πᾶσιν τοῖς διωγμοῖς ὑμῶν
Here, faith in all your persecutions does not mean to believe in or trust in persecutions.
1:5: The evidence that Paul is referring to here is the faithful endurance of the Thessalonian believers while suffering persecution, which he mentioned in verse 4. It may also be helpful to start a new sentence here.

Here, also could mean: (1) the Thessalonian believers are suffering for the kingdom of God as well as being counted worthy of it; (2) the Thessalonian believers are suffering along with other believers.
1:6: παρὰ Θεῷ, ἀνταποδοῦναι τοῖς θλίβουσιν ὑμᾶς θλῖψιν

Here, to return means to cause someone to experience the same thing that they did to someone else as though the same action were bouncing back onto the people who did that action. Use a natural expression for this kind of reciprocal action.
1:7: ἐν τῇ ἀποκαλύψει τοῦ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ
Here, at the revealing is an indication of the time when the suffering believers will have relief from their suffering.
1:8: Here, the ones not having known God refers to those who have refused the relationship with God that he had offered to them.
καὶ τοῖς μὴ ὑπακούουσιν τῷ εὐαγγελίῳ
The phrase, not obeying the gospel could refer to: (1) the same people as those not having known God; (2) a separate group.
The phrase, obeying the gospel is an idiom that means to live according to everything that God tells us in the gospel message.
1:9: Here, the phrase pay the penalty is an idiom meaning to suffer the consequences of doing something bad.
Here, the face of the Lord is an idiom meaning the presence of the Lord.
1:10: ὅταν ἔλθῃ … ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ ἐκείνῃ
Here, that day is the day when Jesus will return to the world.
The saints and the ones having believed are one group of people, not two.
1:11: Paul is using always as an exaggeration in order to emphasize how often he prays for them.
Here, calling refers to God appointing or choosing people to belong to him and to proclaim his message of salvation through Jesus.
1:12: τὸ ὄνομα τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦ
Here, the name of our Lord Jesus stands for the person of the Lord Jesus.
τοῦ Θεοῦ ἡμῶν καὶ Κυρίου Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
The phrase translated as our God and the Lord Jesus Christ could refer to: (1) two persons of the Trinity, God the Father and Jesus the Son. (2) one person, Jesus, who is both God and Lord.
2:1: General Information: In verses 1–12, Paul exhorts believers not to be deceived about the day Jesus will come back and warns them about the coming man of lawlessness. A heading for this section might be, “The Man of Lawlessness” or “The Deception before Jesus Returns.”
2:2: Here, the day of the Lord refers to the time when Jesus will come back to the earth for all believers.
2:3: Here, son of destruction is an idiom meaning a person who is destined for destruction.
God will destroy this person some time after the events of verse 4.
2:4: Here, showing that he himself is God does not mean that this man is God, but only that he is displaying himself to the world as though he were God.
2:5: Paul is not asking for information here, but is using the question form to remind the Thessalonians of what he taught when he was with them previously.
2:6: There are two possibilities for understanding the function of the word now here. (1) It goes with the one restraining {him}; or (2) it goes with you know.
2:7: To restrain someone is to hold him back or to keep him from doing what he wants to do.
Here Paul speaks of the person who is restraining the man of lawlessness as though he were standing in front of him and blocking his path.
2:8: In this figure of speech, breath represents the power of God and mouth represents the spoken word of Jesus.
These two phrases describe the same event. Paul says the same thing twice, in slightly different ways, to emphasize how much more powerful Jesus is than the man of lawlessness.
2:9: Here, whom refers back to the man of lawlessness.
ἐν πάσῃ δυνάμει, καὶ σημείοις, καὶ τέρασιν ψεύδους
Here, all is hyperbole. It can apply to: (1) only power, with the meaning “much” or “great.” or (2) power, signs, and wonders, with the meaning or (3) a combination of the two.
The words signs and wonders often occur together and mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize how amazing they are.
2:10: Here, all is hyperbole and could mean: (1) “a high degree of” or (2) “many kinds of”
2:11: Paul is speaking of God allowing something to happen to people as if he is sending something to them.
2:13: General Information: Paul now changes topics. Suggested heading: “Paul gives thanks to God for the believers and encourages them.”
The word translated Now marks a change in topic.
The word always is a generalization. This is used to emphasize the importance of the action.
Being among the first people to be saved is spoken of as if the Thessalonian believers were firstfruits.
2:14: εἰς περιποίησιν δόξης τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ

The phrase to the acquiring of the glory of our Lord Jesus Christ does not mean that we will take over or divide up the glory of Jesus Christ. It means that the believers will share in Christ’s glory.
2:15: Here, the phrase stand firm is used to mean to not change one’s beliefs but, rather, to remain steadfast in what one believes.
Here, traditions refers to the truths about Christ that Paul and the other apostles taught. Paul speaks of them as if his readers could hold on to them with their hands.
These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The repetition is used to emphasize the importance of doing this.
Here, by word is an expression that means that Paul had been present with them and taught them personally.
2:16: Connecting Statement: Paul ends this section with a blessing.
αὐτὸς … ὁ Κύριος ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦς Χριστὸς
Here, himself gives additional emphasis to the phrase Lord Jesus Christ.
2:17: παρακαλέσαι ὑμῶν τὰς καρδίας, καὶ στηρίξαι
Here, the word hearts represents both the emotion and will of a person.
3:1: General Information: In verses 1–5, Paul asks the believers to pray for him and his companions and encourages them. A heading for this section might be, “Pray for Us.”
Paul speaks of God’s word spreading as if it were running from place to place. He is comparing the rapid spread of God’s word to a person who takes good news to others.
3:2: The two terms perverse and evil mean basically the same thing and are used together to emphasize the amount of evil.
The phrase not everyone is a negative understatement that emphasizes how rare faith is.
3:3: The word strengthen here refers to spiritual strength, not physical strength.
This could mean: (1) the evil being Satan; or (2) evil in general.
3:4: πεποίθαμεν δὲ ἐν Κυρίῳ ἐφ’ ὑμᾶς

This could mean: (1) Paul has confidence in the Thessalonian believers because of the close relationship that they have with the Lord Jesus. In this case, Paul is speaking of this relationship as if they were inside the Lord Jesus; (2) Paul has confidence in the Lord Jesus, that he will cause them to do what is right.
3:5: Here, hearts stands for a person’s thoughts or mind.
Paul speaks of God’s love and Christ’s endurance as if they were destinations on a path.
3:6: General Information: In verses 6–15, Paul gives the believers some final instructions about working and not being idle. A heading for this section might be, “Believers Must Work.”
ἐν ὀνόματι τοῦ Κυρίου ἡμῶν, Ἰησοῦ Χριστοῦ
Here, name stands for the person of Jesus Christ.
Here Paul speaks of people who are not living well as if they walk in a haphazard manner.
Here, the traditions refers to the teachings that the apostles received from Jesus and are passing along to all believers.
3:8: Paul refers to bread here because it was the most common and basic food for them.
Here, toil and hardship have very similar meanings. Paul used this repetition to emphasize that they worked very hard.
3:11: Meddlers are people who interfere in the affairs of others without being asked to help.
3:13: The word you refers to all the Thessalonian believers, so it should be in plural form.
3:14: Paul is referring to his command to the Thessalonian believers as a word.
Paul wants the Thessalonians to notice who this person is.
Paul instructs believers to avoid lazy believers as a disciplinary action.
3:16: General Information: In verses 16–18, Paul makes closing remarks to the believers at Thessalonica. A heading for this section might be, “Closing Remarks.”
αὐτὸς … ὁ Κύριος τῆς εἰρήνης, δῴη ὑμῖν
Paul ends the letter with blessings that are also prayers.
Here, himself emphasizes that the Lord is the source of peace and that he will personally give peace to believers.
3:17: Paul makes it clear that this letter is from him and is not a forgery.
3:18: Paul ends the letter with one more blessing.
